plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three rendered orbital shapes in a row on a white background, each captioned in bold beneath it, reading from left to right "An s orbital", "A p orbital", and "A d orbital". The leftmost is one translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in every direction, with a small yellow-green bead at its center marking the nucleus. The middle shape stacks two lobes vertically, a rounded pink one above and a matching blue one below, meeting at a green nucleus bead; both are drawn as full, doorknob-like volumes rather than pointed teardrops, and they pinch away to nothing where they meet. The rightmost carries four lobes in a cloverleaf around a central green bead, their colors alternating around the ring: pink at the upper left and lower right, blue at the upper right and lower left. Color does the encoding, pink and blue standing for opposite algebraic signs of the wave function across a node, so the alternation shows the sign flipping with each crossing from one lobe to the next. The three together set out the orbital shapes and sign patterns that later account for bonding.

elements: nucleus: a small green bead at the origin
s orbital: one unbroken translucent pink sphere centered on the nucleus
p orbital: two rounded, doorknob-like lobes stacked vertically — pink above, blue below — pinching to nothing at the nucleus
d orbital: four rounded lobes in a planar cloverleaf around the nucleus — pink at upper-left and lower-right, blue at upper-right and lower-left
nodal pinch/pinch points where lobes meet at the nucleus (the node structure)
bold caption beneath the selected orbital reading 'An s orbital', 'A p orbital', or 'A d orbital'

interactions.teaches: Orbital lobes are 3D volumes — rotating the shape shows the p orbital's axis and confirms that the d orbital's cloverleaf lies in one plane

demo_steps.title: An s orbital
demo_steps.narration: The s orbital is a single smooth sphere with no nodes — the wave function has one sign (pink) everywhere.

demo_steps.title: A p orbital
demo_steps.narration: The p orbital stacks two lobes vertically with opposite signs — pink above, blue below — separated by one nodal plane through the nucleus.

demo_steps.title: A d orbital
demo_steps.narration: The d orbital carries four lobes in a cloverleaf; colors alternate around the ring because two perpendicular nodal planes flip the sign at each crossing.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Only one orbital is visible at a time, centered on the origin; nucleus bead at origin, radius ~0.12 world units, opaque green #79a832. s orbital: single sphere radius ~1.2, pink. p orbital: two ellipsoid lobes scaled from unit spheres, long half-axis ~1.15 along ±Y (pink at +Y, blue at -Y), each centered ~0.75 from the origin so they pinch together near the bead — vertical stacking exactly as in the source. d orbital: four ellipsoid lobes lying in the screen XY plane at azimuths 45°, 135°, 225°, 315° (long half-axis ~1.05, centered ~0.7 from origin); pink at 135° (upper-left) and 315° (lower-right), blue at 45° (upper-right) and 225° (lower-left), matching the source alternation. Colors: translucent pink #df9fae and translucent blue #83b5e2, opacity ~0.6, on a white background; pink = positive sign, blue = negative sign. Captions must read exactly 'An s orbital', 'A p orbital', 'A d orbital'.
interactionPlan.notes: Build each lobe as a scaled SphereGeometry (ellipsoid); true spherical-harmonic sampling of |Y| is optional. Use transparent MeshPhongMaterial with depthWrite false to avoid sorting artifacts between overlapping lobes. Click: raycast against lobe meshes, raise emissive on the same-sign group and dim the opposite group; clicking empty space or the same lobe again clears the highlight. On the orbital toggle, show/hide prebuilt orbital groups rather than rebuilding geometry, and update the caption text sprite accordingly.

authoredContext:
What do orbitals look like? There are four different kinds of orbitals, denoted s, p, d, and f, each with a different shape. Of the four, we’ll be concerned primarily with s and p orbitals because these are the most common in organic and biological chemistry. An s orbital has a spherical shape, with the nucleus at its center; a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two parts, or lobes; and four of the five d orbitals have a cloverleaf shape with four lobes, as shown in the figure. The fifth d orbital is shaped like an elongated dumbbell with a doughnut around its middle.

The three different p orbitals within a given shell are oriented in space along mutually perpendicular directions, denoted px, py, and pz. As shown in the figure, the two lobes of each p orbital are separated by a region of zero electron density called a node. Furthermore, the two orbital regions separated by the node have different algebraic signs, + and −, in the wave function, as represented by the different colors in the figure and the figure. As we’ll see in Section 1.11, these algebraic signs for different orbital lobes have important consequences with respect to chemical bonding and chemical reactivity.

Representations of s, p, and d orbitals. An s orbital is spherical, a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and four of the five d orbitals are cloverleaf-shaped. Different lobes of p orbitals are often drawn for convenience as teardrops, but their actual shape is more like that of a doorknob, as indicated.

A characteristic s, p, and d orbital with the nucleus at the center of each. Two cloverleaf-shaped lobes and four cloverleaf-shaped lobes form the p and d orbitals, respectively.

The orbitals in an atom are organized into different layers around the nucleus called electron shells, which are centered around the nucleus and have successively larger size and energy. Different shells contain different numbers and kinds of orbitals, and each orbital within a shell can be occupied by two electrons. The first shell contains only a single s orbital, denoted 1s, and thus holds only 2 electrons. The second shell contains one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals and thus holds a total of 8 electrons. The third shell contains a 3s orbital, three 3p orbitals, and five 3d orbitals, for a total capacity of 18 electrons. These orbital groupings and their energy levels are shown in the figure.

discrepancies: Source shows all three orbitals side-by-side simultaneously; generated figure shows only one at a time behind s/p/d toggle buttons (acceptable as a multipanel toggle, but the comparative composition is lost by default)
Default camera is a tilted axonometric view (axisScreenAngles 30/30), so the p and d orbitals are seen at an angle rather than front-on as in the source, foreshortening the d-orbital cloverleaf
Nucleus bead in the source s orbital is pale yellow-green; generated nucleus is a stronger green
Source p-orbital lobes are slightly teardrop/rounded lobes meeting at the nucleus; generated lobes are symmetric ellipsoids with a visible gap around the nucleus
evaluation.notes: Correct primitives, colors, sign alternation, and captions for all three orbitals with a well-implemented toggle, demo steps, and sign-highlight interaction; main weaknesses are the tilted default view versus the source's front-on presentation and the loss of the side-by-side comparative layout.
action_items: Set the default camera closer to front-on (especially for the p and d orbitals) so the cloverleaf and two-lobe shapes match the source's flat presentation
Add a 'show all' mode or arrange the three orbitals side-by-side to preserve the source's comparative composition
Close the small gap between p-orbital lobes so they meet at the nucleus as in the source
